relevance_note: Single-patient case report of Alexander disease diagnosed by neuropathology, no GFAP testing: 'A case of progressive fibrinoid degeneration of astrocytes is described.'
method_note: Old (pre-GFAP) single-patient case report converted by OCR; two-column text is interleaved line by line, so several sentences are split and spans are given as contiguous fragments (lists) rather than whole sentences. No GFAP testing or variant is reported for anyone, so the variants table is empty; individuals are in scope by diagnosis of Alexander's disease. Publication year is not printed in the file, so year is null. n_patients_reported left null (the field counts patients with a GFAP variant; none). cites_prior_report_of_same_patients left null (paper does not say). Previously published cases from the Discussion were included only when the paper gives an individual-level fact beyond diagnosis: Alexander (1949), Stevenson and Vogel (1952), Crome (1953), Herndon et al. (1970) boy, and the three older-onset cases (Vogel and Hallervorden 1962; Seil et al. 1968; Herndon et al. 1970 adult). Attribution of onset ages to the three older cases, of 'mental retardation' to Stevenson and Vogel, and of the bodies in peripheral nerves to Crome relies on reconstructing the interleaved columns. Herndon onset age printed as '1 ψ years' (OCR damage; probably a fraction), so no ISO value. Not given rows: cases of Wohlwill et al. (1959), Schochet et al. (1968), Garret and Ames (1974), Sherwin and Berthrong (1970), Freide, Iri and Matsuyama (only diagnosis or facts about relatives); the relatives themselves (Wohlwill sibs with 'hydrocephalus' as a group count, a cousin and an uncle with mental retardation, a normal dizygotic twin) were not given rows because they are not described as having Alexander disease or as tested, and the sibs have no individual detail. Group statements ('Eight resembled the present case...', 'nine males and two females', 'In all, except for the biopsy case of Herndon et al., the diagnosis was established by necropsy') were not assigned to individuals; vital status of the older cases was therefore left not reported. Stevenson and Vogel's case recorded deceased at 7 years from 'lived till the age of 7 years'. For the index patient: 'vomiting' is reported once, not as recurrent, so the 'recurrent vomiting' checklist item is not reported. Mental retardation was not mapped to the 'developmental delay' or 'cognitive decline' checklist items. Checklist imaging-type items (white matter, basal ganglia/thalamus) were marked observed from necropsy and histology findings, not imaging. The fontanelles were normal at 9 weeks and later showed increased tension; these are different time points, not a contradiction. The ventriculogram said the ventricles were not dilated, whereas necropsy found dilated lateral (posterior horns) and third ventricles (different time points); the 'not dilated' statement is split across interleaved lines, so no excluded row was made. Normal blood sugar, calcium, urea, tryptophan load test, urinary amino acids and skull radiograph are too fragmented by the interleaving to quote as a contiguous statement, so no excluded rows were made; CSF protein values (1.3 and 2.7 g/l) were not recorded as a feature because the paper does not call them raised. Spinal cord: macroscopically unremarkable but histology notes less severe changes; the medulla/cervical cord checklist item was left not reported. Biopsy was first read as astrocytoma. Tables were built with a short script from my own reading; every span was checked verbatim by script.
